Harry Truman. The thirty-third President of the United States, serving from nineteen forty-five to nineteen fifty-three, Truman ascended to the presidency upon Franklin D. Roosevelt's death during World War Two and inherited the decision to use atomic weapons against Japan. A former senator from Missouri with minimal foreign policy experience, Truman faced the onset of the Cold War, the Korean War, and the complex transition to a postwar order.

Truman was Franklin Roosevelt's vice president for less than one hundred days before Roosevelt's death on April twelfth, nineteen forty-five. He was largely uninformed of the atomic bomb project until becoming president. In August nineteen forty-five, Truman authorized the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, arguing the decision would end the war quickly and avoid a costly invasion of the Japanese mainland. This act remains historically contested and morally weighty.

The Truman Doctrine in nineteen forty-seven pledged American support to nations resisting communist subversion. It provided military and economic aid to Greece and Turkey and established containment as the foundation of Cold War strategy. The Marshall Plan from nineteen forty-eight to nineteen fifty-two provided billions in American aid to rebuild Western Europe, aimed at preventing economic desperation that might enable communist movements.

Truman initiated American membership in the United Nations and backed the creation of Israel in nineteen forty-eight, recognizing the new state despite Arab opposition and strategic complications in the Middle East. The Korean War erupted in nineteen fifty when North Korea invaded the South. Truman committed American troops under UN auspices but controversially dismissed General Douglas MacArthur in nineteen fifty-one over disagreements about war aims and operations in China.

Truman undertook a limited civil rights agenda, including desegregating the military by executive order. He ran a whistle-stop campaign in nineteen forty-eight highlighting his pro-labor, anti-segregation stance and was reelected in a stunning upset over Thomas Dewey.

Truman had access to the atomic bomb and faced numerous Cold War crises including the Berlin Blockade and the Soviet test of an atomic bomb. His willingness to use military force and nuclear deterrence defined the early Cold War era and established precedents that would shape American foreign policy for decades.
